slides.text: I inherited a beautiful, intricate grandfather clock from my grandmother that hadn't ticked in forty years. I brought it to a small, dusty horology shop run by Silas, a quiet man with incredibly sad eyes and gentle hands. Over the next month, I visited his shop every single afternoon, bringing him dark coffee and listening to his deep, soothing voice explain the delicate, hidden gears of time.

I realized I was falling madly in love with him when I started secretly hoping the clock would never be fixed. But yesterday, Silas called. It was done. I arrived at the shop, my heart heavy with the realization that my excuse to see him was entirely gone. The clock ticked perfectly in the corner. I paid him, fighting back hot tears, and awkwardly turned to leave his shop forever.

'Wait,' Silas called out suddenly, his calm voice cracking. He reached deep into his leather apron pocket and pulled out a small, golden gear. 'The clock will stop ticking again in exactly three days,' he confessed, stepping closer to me. 'I purposely left a piece out. I didn't know how else to ask you to come back.' I smiled, dropping my car keys. 'Then you better take it apart again.'
